Unlawful act of architecture · Concepts · Lex Plataformae
<1>Can an infringement lie in the design of an app?</1><2>Unlawful act of architecture</2>
We are used to looking for abuse in a contract clause, in a sentence you can underline and show the judge. But in some cases no single clause, on its own, is the problem.

The problem is the pattern that keeps repeating. Options that come already checked, friction whenever you try to do what you want, manufactured urgency and a cancellation path that seems built to make you give up. And also equivalences that shift whenever it suits the company, punishments that are hard to understand and evidence that is impossible to gather. Each piece seems small. Together, they work as a method.
<1>Unlawful act of architecture</1>

Unlawful means what the law does not accept, and architecture, here, means the design of the service, its screens, paths, built-in rules and punishment systems. That design is also the company's conduct, not a neutral backdrop where things simply happen. So when the design organizes losses in a stable way, the infringement lies in the design. The question is no longer only whether an isolated promise was kept but how the service itself was built to work.

When inducement, extraction and normalization of losses become stably incorporated into the design of the ecosystem, the problem ceases to be merely one of fragmentary nonperformance and comes to constitute a teleological unlawful act of architecture.<1>p. 732</1>
Abusiveness, then, ceases to appear merely as an isolated accident or a severable clause and comes to reside in the very operating program of the service.<1>p. 664</1>
A cutaway building with stairs that only go down, doors that only open inward and windows painted on the wall. No sign forbids anything, and the design traps you.
How can a building forbid without writing anything?
Design speaks. It is a language made of screens, buttons, paths and automatic rules, and this language defines what can be seen, proven, contested, repaired and even remembered.

In a building, the emergency exit can sit behind three locked doors. No one wrote a rule saying it is forbidden to leave. The design settles that before any conversation. Something similar happens with apps, because whoever designs decides a lot before you notice there was anything to decide.

Technique comes to operate as manifest language, that is, fully operative. A language of architecture and engineering that defines what can be seen, proven, contested, repaired and even remembered.<1>p. 32</1>

The second is the layer of architecture and implementation, in which such statements cease to be simple declarations and are converted into a configuration of possibilities by means of interface, flows, access patterns, visibility parameters and technical restrictions that delimit the range of the possible before any interpretive dispute<1>p. 365</1>
Which five pieces form the unlawful act?

Five pieces fit together and keep repeating. Noise in information, which confuses instead of guiding. Friction at the moment of deciding, which pushes you one way. Evidence out of the user's reach. Changes that cannot be checked. And repair that does not cover the loss.

None of them alone makes the unlawful act. The stable combination does. And this avoids two common mistakes. One is accepting that everything is innovation, as if constant change left the platform free to downgrade anything. The other is hunting for isolated clauses, as if the service could only be controlled in pieces of text and never in the way it works.
Which screen traps already have a name?
Some screen traps already have a well-known name, dark patterns. They are the box that comes already checked, the hidden cancellation path and the urgency that pressures you to decide fast.
Is the Consumer Protection Code already enough?

This does not call for a new law or a separate law for platforms. The Brazilian Consumer Protection Code (Código de Defesa do Consumidor, CDC) already has the grammar to see the problem, as long as you look at the program of the service, and not only at the text of the contract.

And the response can reach the source. When the loss comes from the design, fixing one case at a time is not enough. You can ask for the design itself to be corrected, for more transparency, for changes in the service's paths and for measures that reach everyone facing the same problem.

The possible legal qualification extends to structural abusive practice, defect in the supply regime, possible cumulation with a quality defect and grounds for injunctive and corrective protection of architecture.<1>p. 747</1>
Is it the beauty of the screen that is being judged?

Neither the style nor the beauty of the screen is judged. Design can and should organize the experience, because that is what it exists for. What it cannot do is turn this into a stable program of exploitation.

Nor is it about turning every power difference into suspicion, or moralizing economic activity. The category only makes sense when there is a stable pattern, one that repeats and that relevantly affects your practical freedom and what you bought.
What is called into question is not design as style, visual language or interface aesthetics [...]<1>p. 664</1>
[...] the architecture of the service may organize enjoyment, but it cannot do so as a stable program of exploitation.<1>p. 665</1>
It is not a matter of moralizing the exercise of economic activity nor of turning every asymmetry into generic suspicion.<1>p. 664</1>

The category is only justified when the exploitative effect stems from the very design of the flow and of governance, when the mechanism presents itself as a stable and replicable pattern of operation and when this pattern relevantly affects the consumer's practical autonomy and the integrity of enjoyment<1>p. 666</1>
<1><2>7</2>What if the loss is part of the plan?</1>
If the infringement lies in the design, who can see the design from the inside?
When does architecture become an unlawful act?

When governance repeatedly organizes informational noise, decisional friction, evidentiary opacity, non-auditable mutation and insufficient restoration. In this case, unlawfulness no longer lies only in the wording of the contract. The inducement, extraction and normalization of losses become a stable part of the design of the environment, and the case is no longer merely fragmentary nonperformance.
Why is it imputable conduct?

In continuous services that administer immaterial objects of consumption, performance is not exhausted in the contractual text and cannot be understood without the governance that executes it. Architecture is read as conduct, and therefore it can be imputed to the supplier. The service may organize enjoyment through its architecture, but it cannot do so as a stable program of exploitation.
The IOC incorporates this layer, but adds another: the reading of architecture as conduct and of abusive teleology as a design defect of the regime of governed enjoyment.<1>p. 573</1>

In continuous digital services that administer Immaterial Objects of Consumption, performance is not exhausted in the contractual text nor can it be understood without the governance that executes it.<1>p. 664</1>
It is in this sense that the teleological unlawful act of architecture can be qualified as legally imputable conduct.<1>p. 733</1>
What is not at issue?

The examination does not concern style, visual language or interface aesthetics. Nor is there any need to invent a parallel law for platforms, because the qualification is made within the grammar of the CDC.

A vocabulary for contesting

Your skin is a product, but a product of a special kind. You do not take it home, and its use, what it shows others and the place it gives you exist only while the platform keeps the environment running. The legal category of this product is the Immaterial Object of Consumption.

The law of the platform (Lex Plataformae) · Concepts · Lex Plataformae
<1>Who makes the rules inside a platform?</1><2><3>The law of the platform</3><4>Lex Plataformae</4></2>

Inside a platform, someone decides what you can do, what others will see of you and what happens if you break a rule. When you created the account, you accepted the terms of use, and it seems the rules are all there.

But the rules that weigh on your day are not only in the contract nobody reads. They are in the very operation of the app. They are in the paths the screen offers and in those it hides, in the punishments that arrive without warning and in the internal procedures by which the company itself decides conflicts. Whoever wrote the rule is also the one who enforces it and who keeps the records of what happened.

The Lex Plataformae is treated here as the contemporary form of practical normativity exercised through protocols, flows, interfaces, sanctions and private adjudication procedures that organize consumption in an environment.<1>p. 392</1>
<1><2>The law of the platform</2><3>Lex Plataformae</3></1>

The name in Latin is Lex Plataformae, and plataformae means of the platform. It is not a contract sitting in a drawer, but an order that runs as a system, aims at an economic result and seems natural because it is repeated so often. It does not only announce rules. It classifies, records, recommends, blocks, restricts and changes the very environment in which you try to use what you bought. And whenever we talk about the platform that governs the place, we are talking about this law. The name comes from an old expression, the law merchant, used for the rules that traders created among themselves, without depending on the law of any country. The difference is that here the center is not the practice of many traders. It is a single company, which controls the front door, the way you understand what happens and the conditions under which you can use what is yours.
An open rulebook whose pages, seen from behind, are gears running on their own. No one turns the pages, and the book runs.
Why does the platform's rule feel like weather?

Nobody sues the rain. The weather happens and we adjust. The law of the platform works like manufactured weather, which produces the facts of consumption in a predictable sequence, with a shallow explanation and an air of normality.

It also resembles a custom, because what is repeated many times starts to seem agreed by everyone. But on a platform, repetition may be merely the effect of a design the company chose on its own. Once it is shown that all this is organized by design and by punishment, what seemed like weather looks like a decision again, and a decision can be controlled.

Technique comes to operate as manifest language, that is, fully operative. A language of architecture and engineering that defines what can be seen, proven, contested, repaired and even remembered. It manufactures facts of consumption the way one manufactures weather in a predictable sequence, with superficial justification and an appearance of strict normality.<1>p. 32</1>
On the platform, the repetition of practices and solutions should not be read naively as a sufficient sign of normative legitimacy.<1>p. 28</1>
Often, what presents itself as market habit or custom of the ecosystem is already the product of unilateral design<1>p. 28</1>
What are the three layers of the law of the platform?
The law of the platform works in three layers, one on top of the other.

The first is the text, with the terms of use, the conduct policies, the moderation rules and the criteria for taking part. The second is the design, which turns the text into screens, paths, access limits and visibility criteria, and decides what is possible before any discussion. If the screen has no button, it does not matter that the contract allows it. The third is enforcement, which grades punishments, cuts visibility, suspends functions and, at the extreme, expels.
A rule only really bites when it passes through all three layers, because only then does it change what you can do and what happens to you.
How does an Honor system become a rule?

In an online game, the company created an Honor system, in which behavior becomes a score. Those who behave in a sportsmanlike way earn benefits. Those who behave badly receive fewer rewards and lose part of the right to speak in chat.

When you are punished, with a temporary suspension or a chat restriction, your score drops, your progress stalls and the account goes without certain rewards until you show, consistently, that you have changed. None of this goes through a court. The punishment is built into the system and affects what you can do, earn and show. And since the company builds the game, measures the matches and sets the punishment criteria without showing how they work, the question in a conflict is not only whether you broke a rule. It is also whether the criteria used to say so are legitimate.
If the rule that counts is the one that is running, what changes?
When the rule that counts is the one that is running, the dispute is no longer only about the text of the contract. It becomes a dispute about who governs what can be done in there.

This changes what you can ask for. If the platform exercises this kind of power, it needs limits proportional to it. Among them are transparency that actually serves a purpose, a minimum of stability, reasons you can check, a real way to contest and the restoration of what was lost.
Does the law of the platform replace the laws of the country?

This does not make the platform a State, nor does it place it above the law of the country. The law of the platform does not replace Brazilian law. It is a layer of private rules that sits between you and what you bought, and that the law cannot treat as a mere technical setting. Nor is it about taking any game dispute to the Constitution.
Here the point is not to convert the platform into a State [...]<1>p. 366</1>
<1><2>4</2>Who is in charge after the purchase?</1>
If the platform writes the rule and also carries it out, who checks what it does?
What is the law of the platform?

It is a private ordering, and not a set of predisposed clauses. It is technically executable, economically oriented and semiotically naturalized. Its institutional core is the platform, which defines rules, visibilities, sanctions and evidentiary regimes through continuous architecture and updating, based on curation, sanction and unilateral mutation.

Rule, implementation and enforcement organize participation, visibility and sanction, with a direct effect on the position of enjoyment that gives the IOC its economic value. Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC) · Concepts · Lex Plataformae
<1>What do you receive when you pay for something digital?</1><2>Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC)</2>
Anyone who buys a refrigerator takes it home. From then on, it works far from the seller, and the store only comes back into the story if a defect shows up.

Much of what is digital does not work that way. Anyone who buys an item in a game, a subscription in an app or access to a platform also buys something. But using it still depends, every day, on an environment that the company maintains, adjusts and can change. What you have works only on the inside, under the rules of whoever runs the place.

The old rules were designed for stable things, delivered all at once, with defects you can spot by looking. On their own, they cannot cope with a product that keeps being tinkered with after the sale. What decides whether you are in this kind of situation is not whether the item is digital, nor what the company calls it. It is how much what you use depends on the environment the platform governs.

The problem can no longer be satisfactorily grasped by the classical grammar of the product or the service, conceived under assumptions of stability, one-off delivery and a defect knowable by relatively direct inspection.<1>p. 501</1>
<1>Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC)</1>

It is the legal category for this kind of product. What counts in it is not only the image on the screen, but the position of use you come to occupy, which the platform sustains day after day. The category does not say you bought less. It says you bought a product, in the sense of consumer law, whose supply continues after the purchase. The service the platform provides does not erase the product. It is precisely how what was sold is maintained, updated and shaped.

What is asserted is that, whenever the consumed utility presents itself as a position of enjoyment sustained by continuous private governance, there will be an immaterial product in a legally relevant sense for the application of art. 3, § 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>.<3>p. 718</3>
From this angle, the qualification of the IOC as an immaterial product does not require denying the service dimension of the relationship.<1>p. 718</1>
An empty lot marked out with stakes and string, overgrown with weeds, and in the middle of it the frame of a building starting to rise.
What lot did the law mark out in 1990?

The law marked out a lot in 1990, when the Consumer Protection Code said that a product can be immaterial. The space was reserved, but criteria still had to be built on it for products that depend on a platform that keeps controlling them.

The Immaterial Object of Consumption is the building on that lot. And an empty lot has a cost. While a loss lacks a category and a criterion, it is hard to show and to claim, and every gap that lasts tends to become someone's business model.
By giving legal density to what was merely a residual label, the IOC prevents immateriality from functioning as an alibi for the technical irresponsibility of platforms.<1>p. 25</1>
It produces predictable institutional effects, because every stable dogmatic gap tends to be converted into a business model<1>p. 25</1>
How can you tell whether your case is covered?
Four questions help you recognize an immaterial object of consumption, and the answer to all four must be yes.

The first is what was promised. It is not enough to say that some content was available. You need to say which utility was sold, what it was supposed to let you do and what it was supposed to mean, and you will not find that in slogans or decorative lists.

The second is whether the purchase opened a position that lasts. Buying, here, does not mean receiving a package and being done. It means gaining a place in an environment that has to keep existing for the thing to be of any use.

The third is whether the platform really governs that place. Having technology involved is not enough. There must be internal rules, choices about what appears, participation criteria and punishments that shape your use and have consequences for you.

The fourth is whether the thing can get worse without disappearing. This is the case where access continues, but what you had is downgraded, emptied or reorganized against what was promised, in a serious and lasting way.
The second field is the sustained position of enjoyment.<1>p. 428</1>
The third field is infrastructural governance as the mode of executing supply.<1>p. 428</1>

Infrastructure is incorporated as a constitutive dimension of delivery, because it is through it that internal rules, curation, modulations of visibility, participation parameters and sanction mechanisms are implemented<1>p. 428</1>
The fourth field is the typical possibility of relevant degradation without total rupture.<1>p. 429</1>
Why is the account the portrait of the whole problem?

In an online game, the account gathers characters, skins, emotes and the game's currency, and none of it can leave the account. It is more than a login and password. It is where your inventory, progress, player name and the signals by which others recognize you are kept together.

The account organizes your access, but does not give you possession of the content, which still depends on the environment and on the company's rules. When the game goes down, what is in the account is useless until it comes back. That is why the account can be seen as the central immaterial object of consumption, a miniature portrait of the whole category.
It is not reducible to a login credential. It is the organizational point that holds the enjoyment bundle together<1>p. 408</1>
since it organizes the practical ownership of access, but does not consolidate a regime of consumer possession over the content<1>p. 408</1>
For this reason, it can be described as the central IOC and, at the same time, as a “concept-infrastructure” in miniature.<1>p. 409</1>
What does the law see once the problem is qualified?
Giving a name changes what the law can see, and this has an effect in two places.

In the first, the company can no longer pull the case out of consumer law just by saying that it provides a service or granted a license. Those words are not enough to make what you bought precarious.

In the second, the discussion shifts its center. Instead of looking only at the contract you accepted one day, the focus is on the use you make, every day, of what you bought. The contract still matters, but it does not on its own explain a relationship that plays out all the time through means that go far beyond the text. So being immaterial no longer works as an excuse for the platform not to answer for what it delivers.

The consequence of this qualification is relevant on two planes. On the first, it prevents legal control from being neutralized by the supplier's descriptive strategies, especially by the claim that there would be only the provision of a service or a mere content license, as if these formulas sufficed to naturalize the precariousness of the bond and set aside the protective regime applicable to enjoyment.<1>p. 718</1>

On the second, it redefines the reading axis of the CDC. Instead of operating primarily from the contract as a formal statement, the discipline comes to be structured from enjoyment as a governed relationship.<1>p. 718</1>

This does not mean denying the relevance of the contract, but refusing its explanatory sufficiency in environments in which the economic content of the relationship is carried out continuously by mechanisms that far exceed the contractual text.<1>p. 718</1>
By giving legal density to what was merely a residual label, the IOC prevents immateriality from functioning as an alibi for the technical irresponsibility of platforms<1>p. 25</1>
Which cases fall outside the category?
Not everything becomes a case, and it helps to know where the category ends before you complain.

A service that happens once and ends there, with no lasting position, does not need the category, because the ordinary rules for services settle it. A platform that only works as a shop window or channel, without really governing what you use, also tends to fall outside.

Purely cosmetic changes, when symbolic value was not at the core of what was sold, as a rule also fall outside. And the mere existence of moderation, rankings, community rules or screen adjustments is not enough. Ordinary updates, regular curation and anti-fraud measures are part of the normal life of the service. What counts is a serious and lasting decline in what was promised.
The mere existence of moderation, rankings, community rules or interface adjustments is not enough to trigger the IOC operator.<1>p. 430</1>

Ordinary updates, regular curation, anti-abuse interventions and changes that do not affect the functional core of the enjoyment bundle remain within the normal field of performance and do not by definition constitute relevant degradation.<1>p. 430</1>

The resulting legal qualification is that of an immaterial product subject to the regime of art. 3, § 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, without the service dimension of the bond setting aside the control of enjoyment as the core of supply.<3>p. 743</3>
So when does a change stop being routine and become a loss?
When is there an Immaterial Object of Consumption?

There is an Immaterial Object of Consumption whenever the consumed utility presents itself as a position of enjoyment sustained by continuous private governance. In that case there is an immaterial product in a legally relevant sense, and Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC applies<1><2>1</2></1>. The category gives concrete form to the notion of immaterial product that the law already provided for and reads it as a governed enjoyment bundle.
What decides is not the materiality of the medium, nor the name the supplier gives to what it sells. What decides is the structural dependence of enjoyment on a governed environment.

Abusive teleology · Concepts · Lex Plataformae
<1>What if the way the service works points toward exploiting the people who use it?</1><2>Abusive teleology</2>
Sometimes the problem is not an error, a failure or an isolated case. It is the very way the service works.

Staged scarcity, manufactured urgency, the promise of progress, the threat of losing what you have collected and small downgrades in utility seem trivial when you look at them one by one. Together, they squeeze the time you have to think, raise the cost of leaving, make it harder to turn back and leave you more and more tied to the place. Exploitation almost never shows up in an outrageous clause. It shows up as the way the service is programmed to run, and loss becomes routine.
<1>Abusive teleology</1>

Teleology means purpose, what a thing points toward. The purpose is abusive when the way the service is provided comes, in practice, to point toward exploiting the fragility of its users. Or toward hiding what is lost, or toward turning each change into a way to lock people in and charge them. The decisive point is that no one has to guess at intentions. Nobody investigates what was going on in anyone's head at the company. What matters is the purpose that shows in the operation itself, through the pattern that repeats, the coherence among the pieces and the effect produced again and again.
A staircase seen from the side, in which one step of each flight is always higher than the others. A ruler held against it shows that the difference repeats, always in the same place.
Accident or design?

A stumble on a staircase is an accident. A staircase in which one step in every flight is always higher than the others is design. To see this, no one needs to ask what the engineer was thinking. All it takes is to measure the steps and see that the difference repeats, always in the same place.

It is the same with a digital service. A single episode may be just a failure. When the same pieces combine in the same way, cycle after cycle, and always produce the same kind of loss, what appears is a program, and it is the program that can be examined.
The unlawful act therefore does not arise from a singular episode that can be treated as an accident.<1>p. 666</1>
Which five questions separate abusive purpose from the rest?
To keep it from becoming a catch-all label, abusive purpose has to pass a five-question test, and every answer must be yes.

Is the purpose written into the design itself, in the terms of use, the access rules and the way of punishing, and not just a side effect? Does it repeat as a pattern, instead of being an isolated episode? Does it take advantage of disadvantages that are part of the arrangement, such as the difficulty of understanding, the dependence of those who have already invested a lot, the cost of switching games and the loss of reputation and history? Does it come with a lack of clarity and little chance to contest the decisions that matter? And does it seriously and lastingly affect what you bought, even without taking everything at once?
The fourth requirement is opacity combined with low contestability. It is not enough that the system is complex or operates with metrics.<1>p. 455</1>
A one-off case or part of a pattern?

A skin is sold as exclusive, with the exclusivity built into the price. Months later, it comes back in an alternative shop, in a special currency or for much less, without the duration of the exclusivity having been explained at the time of purchase.

Seen on its own, this may already be misleading advertising by omission. Seen as part of a pattern, in which scarcity is created, sold and then undone cycle after cycle, it may also be a sign of abusive purpose. Artificial scarcity stops being just a commercial strategy when the correspondence between what was promised and what was delivered is hidden or frustrated.
element of abusive teleology<1>p. 745</1>
Why look at the design, and not at intent?

The focus moves from the businessperson's head to the design. That makes the problem demonstrable, because design can be shown through screens, rules, change history and repeated effects, while intent is something no one can prove from the outside.

And the response can go beyond your own case. When the loss stems from the way the service is programmed, you can ask for the game's paths to be redone, for more transparency and for the design to be corrected, including through collective measures.
It is not a matter of investigating the subjective psychological intent of business agents, nor of moralizing every form of monetization, persuasion or private governance.<1>p. 732</1>
Is charging and persuading already abuse?

Nor is it a label for everything. Charging, persuading and governing a game are not abuses in themselves. A merely aggressive business, a debatable design or an arrangement that is simply efficient for the company are not enough either.

The platform also has legitimate purposes, such as security, stability and game balance. Abusive purpose only appears when it can be shown, with reasons, that the design points mainly toward exploiting the fragility of its users and capturing value disproportionately, and not toward those ends.
How do you tell an aggressive business from one whose operation points toward exploitation?
What characterizes abusive teleology?

It is a qualified form of unlawfulness under the CDC regime. The exploitation of vulnerability does not appear as an episodic deviation in the service, but as a purpose built into its operating program. The practical purpose of the arrangement departs from tolerable limits and steers the environment toward the structural exploitation of vulnerability, toward the significant obscuring of enjoyment or toward the recurring use of mutability as a technology of capture.

It depends on two categories that must already be in place. Without the asymmetry it exploits and without the enjoyment bundle it degrades, there is no legally capturable abusive teleology. It reaches exploitative purposes inscribed in the technical and organizational design of the service, and not only in written contractual terms.

Abusive teleology occupies this place as an unlawful act of architecture, that is, as a mode of imputation that reaches exploitative purposes inscribed in the technical-organizational design of the service, and not only in textual contractual commands.<1>p. 394</1>

The most appropriate response is usually to fix what failed, not just to pay for the damage. It may be possible to demand records that can be checked, a review of how the service communicates and the restoration of the trust that was lost.
In the most serious cases, when the lack of transparency stops being a technical leftover and becomes part of the way the service is exploited, the very purpose of the design may come into question.

The most appropriate institutional response will tend to favor procedural correction, stronger verifiable trails, a review of the communicational arrangement and functional restoration of the injured trust, rather than the mere abstract monetization of the conflict.<1>p. 760</1>

How does this family govern enjoyment?

Whether the regime applies does not depend on the label of artificial intelligence, assistant or chat. It depends on the governance that modulates, over time, the utility delivered and the possibility of reconstructing promise, alteration and impact. The service is not exhausted in a single answer. It is an environment of cognitive guidance, in which selection, wording, prioritization, synthesis and interface language shape how the user understands the problem and trusts the result. The conflict cannot be reduced to an isolated factual error or to the vocabulary of software licensing.
The service is valuable not only because it answers, but because it induces the user to treat the answer as a relevant point of orientation.<1>p. 758</1>

The application of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption to services of cognitive functionality is not defined by the label of “artificial intelligence”, “assistant”, “chat” or “productivity tool”, but by the governance structure that modulates, over time, the utility delivered and the possibility of reconstructing promise, alteration and functional impact through accessible evidence.<1>p. 757</1>
Which vulnerability does the service trigger?

It is semiotic vulnerability intensified by epistemic dependence. The environment administers the signs of reliability, usefulness and sufficiency of the answer without giving the recipient the same means of verification. The inadequacy may appear as informational noise, when the answer projects a confidence incompatible with the real limits. As functional opacity, when it is impossible to reconstruct why the output was presented or whether the system's behavior changed. And as evidentiary asymmetry, when the impact depends on history and parameters concentrated in the supplier.

No. Games are where these concepts were first tested, because everything shows more clearly there. The account, the currency, the penalties and the changes are in plain view of any player. Outside games, the same effects are usually presented as inevitable, and that is why they are harder to see.

What unites the cases is not the sector of the economy or the type of technology. It is the mechanism by which the platform organizes, adjusts and remakes the experience of those who use it, and makes contesting it easier or harder. That is why it does not matter whether the service is called an app, a store, a network or an assistant. What matters is how it governs what you use.

Four platform families show different faces of the same problem. In each one, the questions are the same. How does the platform govern use? What do the people there depend on? What can be proven and what stays hidden? And what response makes sense when something goes wrong?
The difference is that, outside the game, the same effects tend to be presented as inevitable, rather than as architectural choices<1>p. 23</1>

The unit of examination lies not in the economic sector or in the marketing label of the service, but in the predominant mechanism by which the user's experience is organized, modulated, reconfigured or made contestable.<1>p. 755</1>
It is this mechanism, and not the name of the sector, that provides the basis for comparability<1>p. 755</1>

Each of them makes it possible to observe how the same grid of controllability behaves in the face of specific problems of promise, trust, opacity, mutability, sanction, reputation, intermediation or administration of expectation.<1>p. 757</1>

Why compare platforms by their mechanism?

The criterion of comparison is structural. The unit of examination lies not in the economic sector or in the label of the service, but in the predominant mechanism by which the experience is organized, modulated, reconfigured or made contestable. That keeps the typology from turning into a catalog of markets or depending on the interpreter's cultural familiarity with the environment.

Not every platform reproduces, with the same intensity, the same vulnerability, opacity or capture. What is checked is whether the regime retains recognizable application to typical models of continuous supply.

What matters is not whether the platform presents itself as a cognitive tool, market infrastructure, productive environment or reputation system, but how it organizes access, modulates expectations, distributes risks and conditions the possibility of institutional reconstruction of the conflict.<1>p. 756</1>
